newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Greens upstage Waigel, SPD with tax plan.
newsitem.headline: German Greens upstage Waigel, SPD with tax plan.

text.p: Germany's opposition Greens party on Wednesday sought to shake the political establishment out of its torpor by publishing its own fully-costed plan to reform the country's creaking tax system.
By proposing to cut income tax and simplify tax collection the Greens upstaged their Social Democrat (SPD) allies, who have still not published a complete tax policy of their own.
And the environmentalist party said its revenue-neutral blueprint avoided falling into the "tax-cutting lie" they said was being peddled by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
"Our goal is that there will be a lot of winners and only a few losers," Greens finance spokeswoman Christine Scheel told a news conference.

The Greens' tax programme was timed to show up Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party coalition and the opposition SPD at the most opportune moment -- just after they had again failed to find a compromise on tax reforms.
The two sides met on Tuesday to seek a compromise. But all they could agree on was to meet again next Wednesday in a bid to avert deadlock later in parliament.

Although the Greens only enjoy the support of between 11 and 13 percent of voters in opinion polls, their ideas could carry more weight as they could end up in government in a "red-green" coalition with the SPD after elections next year.
The Greens' scheme lifts elements of Waigel's own plan to cut 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) in income and corporate taxes which would be partly offset by abolishing some 70 tax breaks.

It proposes more moderate income tax cuts than Waigel, lowering the bottom rate to 18.5 percent from 25.9 now. The tax rate would rise in a straight line to a peak of 45 percent on incomes of 120,000 marks, down from 53 percent.
Families and workers on low- and middle incomes should also benefit from a 3,000 mark increase in tax-free allowances to 15,000 marks and a rise in monthly child benefits to 300 marks from 220 marks.

The Greens' plan would also make a small cut in tax on commercial incomes to 45 percent from 47 percent, while taxes on company profits would be unified with that on all capital earnings at 35 percent.
The gross tax cuts would total around 100 billion marks, and would be fully offset by even more sweeping attacks on tax exemptions than those envisaged by Waigel, Scheel said.

The Greens support government plans to end tax relief on "anti-social" shift hours, jobless benefits and travel allowances -- all of which have been opposed by the SPD. Their plan goes further than the coalition's by proposing to tax pensions fully.
Flanking the tax reform, the Greens called for high German occupational insurance charges to be sharply cut and financed by a big increase in petrol tax, something the SPD also wants.

Reacting to the Greens' proposal, SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss praised elements which he said had been taken over from his own party's policies. But he said proposals to hike tax allowances and child benefits went too far to be prudent.
Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) said the Greens were showing the SPD the way by proposing tax cuts.
But, FDP finance spokeswoman Gisela Frick said: "With demands for billions of marks in more spending the Greens won't create a single new job."
